item.title: 5 Ways Nature Nourishes Our Emotions
item.description:
Environment

5 Ways Nature Nourishes Our Emotions

The science behind why nature feels so good.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Research continues to reveal the mechanisms of nature’s physiological and psychological benefits for humans.
  • Time in nature has benefits for various psychoneuroimmunological processes.
  • Contact with nature promotes sleep, exercise and microbiome health.
Source: Radosław Cieśla /Pixabay

Of all the mood-boosting interventions at our disposal, there is one that may be most native to us: spending time in nature. A stroll through the autumn woods in crisp, fresh air, under a spotless blue sky, serenaded by wistful robins, with a carpet of red and yellow leaves under our feet does something indisputable to the body and soul.

We know, almost instinctively, that nature is good for us. What research is now revealing is just what exactly happens when we step into communion with it.

Three main theories shed light on nature’s physiological and psychological benefits.

Attention Restoration Theory takes the route of attention. Our capacity for directed attention is often under strain in our cognitively demanding modern lives. Yet, there is something about being in natural settings that restores this limited and easily depleted resource. In nature, we attend to the surrounding world in a gentler way (researchers call this “soft fascination”), thus replenishing our attentional capacities, which in turn benefit concentration, working memory and other cognitive functions that rely on them. Stress Recovery Theory holds that being in nature can help the body recuperate from stress by activating the parasympathetic nervous system – the branch of the nervous system that is associated with rest and recovery. Studies, for example, show how the resulting benefits of stress reduction show up in our biology, including improvements in measurements of blood pressure, cortisol and heart rate. Finally, the Biophilia Hypothesis points to the evolutionary origins of our affinity for nature. We seek out nature and we enjoy being in its presence. This inherent bond with nature has helped us survive and thrive as a species.

Researchers have also been using neuroimaging modalities such as EEG and fMRI to track nature’s effects on brain function. A recent analysis of such studies found distinct neurophysiological signatures of nature contact, often involving patterns indicating reduced stress, improved attentional control and better emotion regulation. In fact, when it comes to our emotional lives, nature can play a particularly formidable role – reducing negative affect, anxiety, loneliness, depressive symptoms and burnout, and boosting positive affect, a sense of meaning, self-worth, awe and wonder.

How do these effects happen?

In a recent review published in Trends in Cognitive Sciences, Gregory Bratman and James Gross (2026) identify five pathways as possible mechanisms behind the positive effects of nature contact on affective functioning.

Source: Bratman, G. N., & Gross, J. J. (2026). Why nature contact is good for us. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 30(8), 738-751.

1. Emotion regulation

Emotion regulation is the multifaceted process behind the what, when, and how of our efforts to shape our feelings. According to the process model of emotion regulation, this includes five distinct processes: situation selection (choosing which situations to enter), situation modification (changing the situation in order to align with our emotional goals), attentional deployment (where and how we direct our attention), cognitive change (reframing the way we think about a situation), and response modulation (how we try to shape our emotional response).

Nature contact can influence each of these aspects. For example, as the authors point out, people often seek out natural spaces such as parks and watersides, in part because they expect to feel positive emotions there (situation selection). Being in nature is also associated with less rumination (attentional deployment).

2. Psychoneuroimmunology

The mutual influence of mind and body processes is well established. Psychoneuroimmunology frameworks like the Social Safety Theory describe how our emotions – whether positive or negative – affect immune function and inflammation in the body, while inflammatory cytokines may in turn impact our emotions. When the body is in a state of stress and senses or anticipates threat, the immunological response ramps up. While heightened activation can be adaptive in the short run, it becomes harmful when chronically switched on. Here, too, nature contact may offer help. For example, inhaling certain volatile organic compounds that are emitted from trees may have anti-inflammatory effects on the body. Some studies have also found that nature exposure can have positive immunological effects through reductions in interleukin-6 (a pro-inflammatory molecule that when chronically elevated is implicated in autoimmune and inflammatory disorders), and increases in natural killer cells (white blood cells that destroy virus-infected and malignant cells).

3. Human microbiome

The microbes in our gut (“the hidden kingdom”) influence many aspects of our biological health, including hormonal, immune and neural processes. Thanks to the workings of the gut-brain axis, they also affect how we feel. Being in nature, having skin contact with soil or other natural elements, or inhaling airborne microbes can impact the diversity and composition of the microbiome. For example, a two-year biodiversity intervention study from Finland found that children whose playgrounds were enriched with natural elements gained more beneficial microbes on their skin and lost potentially harmful bacteria compared to controls.

4. Sleep

Most of us have personal evidence of how sleep affects our emotions. How often, for example, has poor sleep played havoc with some or other aspect of our affective functioning – from the kinds of emotions we experience during the day, to our success at regulating them? Nature has been called “an environmental determinant” of sleep health. Living near green spaces is associated with better quality and duration of sleep, while nature visits have been associated with fewer nights of insufficient sleep.

5. Physical activity

Physical activity benefits many aspects of our subjective well-being, including our affective health. It does so by increasing positive emotions, decreasing negative emotions and helping us use more adaptive emotion regulation strategies. As Bratman and Gross (2026) write, natural environments are predictors of physical activity for a variety of reasons – from removing obstacles to movement, to making exercise more enjoyable.

The paths that nature takes to exert its beneficial effects on humans are many and mysterious. Much remains to be uncovered by science. This makes the stroll through the autumn woods all the more magical.

item.title: Is It Over? Detecting Romantic Disengagement
item.description:
Relationships

Is It Over? Detecting Romantic Disengagement

Recognizing the signs of impending dissolution.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • The best predictor of emotional disengagement is emotional withdrawal.
  • Healthy relationships contain daily supportive behaviors and communication responsiveness.
  • Digital communication can create emotional distance through ambiguity and asynchronous responding.

Having dating someone for a period of time, you might reach a point where you sense things are different. Perhaps you feel more insecure or anxious, or no longer view a future together with any confidence. Your friends and family notice a change in demeanor or behavior. You appear preoccupied or unsettled, frequently checking your text messages or emails—often to see if your significant other opened the last message you sent, wondering why he or she didn’t respond. When the silence is deafening, it is time to determine whether the bloom is off the rose. Research explains.

Source: Image by Мария Ткачук from Pixabay

Detecting Disengagement From a Relationship

Molly Schwarzenberger et al. (2025) explored how to detect emotional disengagement by investigating machine learning models that were able to accurately identify behavioral, psychological, and communication-related indicators.[i] Studying 156 Canadian couples, they found the best predictor of emotional disengagement was emotional withdrawal, followed by daily supportive behaviors, communication responsiveness, attachment avoidance, and conflict frequency.

In terms of detecting signs of trouble, Schwarzenberger et al. acknowledge that digital environments complicate emotional dynamics. They describe some of the challenges involved with moving in-person communication online, including textual ambiguity and asynchronous responding, which can create emotional distancing, misunderstanding, and unstable expectations of intimacy. They also cite the prevalence of “phubbing,” where one partner uses a smartphone during interpersonal interactions, as a practice which can increase emotional loneliness and decrease relational satisfaction, also contributing to disengagement.

On the topic of technology, Schwarzenberger et al. note that online disinhibition, where people exercise less restraint in digital spaces, is associated with morally disengaged behavior, which in turn can erode trust and prompt emotional withdrawal within romantic relationships. Moral disengagement may also spread from digital spaces into personal relationship dynamics, with partners justifying avoidant behaviors or engaging in emotional neglect, leading to continuing relational decline. As this process continues, they note that emotional disengagement can create mood fluctuations, relational distress, and concerns with underlying mental health.

Acknowledging When the Relationship Is Fading

Schwarzenberger et al. describe the warning signs of emotional disengagement as including emotional withdrawal, as well as decreased daily support and responsive communication. They note that disengagement occurs gradually, with early signs detectable through diminished expressions of empathy, increased avoidance, and reduced relational presence. They describe emotional withdrawal as a defining feature of relational disconnection, and a precursor to decreasing intimacy.

As many ex-couples can attest, disengagement is a process. Schwarzenberger et al. explain that because emotional intimacy is sustained over time through communication responsiveness and daily supportive behaviors, a reduction in these behaviors reduces emotional intimacy. They explain that disengagement is more likely when partners decrease supportive behaviors, which also weakens relational self-esteem.

The bottom line appears to be the importance of recognizing signs of impending relational doom sooner rather than later, with time to decide whether the relationship is worth saving, or if you should throw in the towel. Remaining attuned to relational comfort, satisfaction, and quality will allow you to detect red flags of relationship demise sooner rather than later.

item.title: Habit Change Can Be Difficult. Where Should We Start?
item.description:
Habit Formation

Habit Change Can Be Difficult. Where Should We Start?

Learn how to choose a realistic habit change and break it into manageable steps.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Habits develop when there is a reward that gets attached to a cue.
  • The cue for a habit can be very difficult to determine.
  • Understanding the complexities of habits can lead to successful changes.
Source: Lidiia Moor | iStock

A healthy lifestyle is an accumulation of the choices we make on a regular basis. Many of us know we should be eating right, getting enough exercise, ditching tobacco, and going easy on the alcohol, but it can be difficult. If we take stock of our current habits, we may find we are falling short.

What happens when we want to ditch some of our unhealthy habits for healthier ones? Where do we start? How can we move past “I’ll start tomorrow”?

Habits Are Complicated

First, let’s look at the definition of habit from the American Psychological Association (APA), which defines it as “a well-learned behavior or automatic sequence of behaviors that is relatively situation-specific and over time has become motorically reflexive and independent of motivational or cognitive influence—that is, it is performed with little or no conscious intent.”

This definition gives us an inkling of the complexities involved.

Habits become strong when we are in a stable, consistent environment. That is why it is often suggested that, in order to change a habit, we should try to change our environment to make the change easier.

Some programs have had success with this approach. For instance, replacing soda machines in schools with readily available water, creating more bike paths in cities, placing advertising restrictions on tobacco products, implementing taxes on alcohol, or even measuring waistlines to combat metabolic syndrome (an initiative in Japan).

Habits Often Start With a Cue

Those programs showed some success because many of our habitual behaviors and choices occur in response to cues. James Clear, in his book Atomic Habits, notes that often a habit starts with a cue, followed by a craving. That craving produces a response that is perceived as a reward. The habit gets reinforced. Change the cue, and you can change the response. But what happens when the cue isn’t obvious?

Our environments are layered with cues, many of which are difficult to control or go unnoticed—things like socioeconomic status, education, the family and social cultures we are part of, mental health, genetics, our food environment, and the advertising of unhealthy foods.

Some cues, as noted by the APA, bring about an action that is performed with little or no conscious intent. In other words, between our complex environment and our nearly unconscious response to it, sorting out what cues a specific habit can be very difficult.

Even if we have specific goals and intentions, they are often subsumed by the cues around us. We may start out with a goal to cut back on wine or beer, only to find ourselves in a social situation where alcohol consumption is the norm. People can easily lose sight of their goals when tossed around in a sea of cues that do not support them.

Other Barriers to Habit Change

There are deeper emotional needs that can also drive a habit. According to Clear, some of our choices serve to reduce anxiety, win social approval, or achieve status in the eyes of those around us. Those needs can be difficult or impossible to identify.

Jeremy Dean, in his book Making Habits, Breaking Habits, notes that people often succumb to what he calls a planning fallacy. They think that changing a particular habit will be easier than it actually is. When difficulties ensue, the intent to change the habit gets lost.

Another potential problem is trying to change too much at once. If we try to reshape our lifestyle all at once, or even a significant portion of it, it is likely to backfire. For example, deciding to follow a diet that represents a drastic change from one's usual habits around food may work for a while, but it can turn out to be unsustainable.

Choosing a Habit to Change

Given all this, how can we choose a habit to change that we can succeed at?

Here are some pieces of the puzzle that can aid in the adoption of some new, healthier habits.

  1. Think carefully about what is really possible. One way to do that is to visualize what steps would be involved in the process. Picture yourself completing each step.
  2. Recognize there are many things in your environment that you can’t control. Focus on what you can control, and how you can control those things.
  3. Break down large habits into small ones. Keep getting smaller until you can see yourself accomplishing that change easily. You can always add others later. One success leads to the next one.
  4. Remind yourself of your goals. They can easily get lost in the shuffle of our complex environments and lives.
  5. Identify hidden rewards and trade-offs. Some habits (probably most) will come at the expense of another firmly ingrained habit that brings some kind of reward. Do your best to identify what that reward is, and design a replacement that supports the healthier habit. This is an especially hard one. First, you have to figure out what the previous habit is doing for you, and then replace it with a different desire. Sometimes, cognitive behavioral therapy or coaching can help sort that out.

Habit change is a difficult but rewarding process. If we can acknowledge and work with the difficulties, it will help us design some changes that can lead to better health.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Why the Increase in Global Reports of Mystical Experiences?
item.description:
Spirituality

Why the Increase in Global Reports of Mystical Experiences?

5 mystical pathways suggest a new understanding of humanity's future.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Mystical experiences recur across cultures and centuries through five different pathways.
  • These experiences often involve profound love, unity, and interconnectedness.
  • Resuscitation technology and psychedelics for psychiatric problems have increased reports of the mystical.

A friend of mine ate a chicken sandwich in a restaurant, walked into the parking lot, and had a mystical experience.

How does something so extraordinary happen in such an ordinary setting? What does his experience have in common with people who have spent decades meditating, taken psychedelics, survived encounters with death, or participated in experimental virtual reality? I have become fascinated by worldwide reports of mystical experiences across cultures and centuries, through remarkably different pathways.

Reports of mystical experiences are becoming more numerous and more systematically documented, partly because of advances in medical resuscitation and renewed research into psychedelics. More people now survive close encounters with death and can describe their experiences, which strongly resemble previously reported mystical experiences. At the same time, researchers are studying psilocybin and other psychedelics as potential treatments for depression, anxiety, addiction, and other psychiatric conditions. These developments are bringing experiences once studied primarily within religious and spiritual traditions into increasingly systematic scientific investigation.

Source: Pexels / Pixabay

What Is a Mystical Experience?

Imagine standing beneath a tree and suddenly experiencing yourself, the tree, the ground, and the surrounding landscape as parts of one living reality. The boundaries separating you from the world seem to disappear (Stace, 1960). Intense love expands into what feels like the Universe or God. People describe profound peace, joy, gratitude, awe, and sacredness. Time may expand into an endless present. William James (1902) added Ineffability, difficulty putting these experiences into words and noetic quality, the sense of directly knowing something profound.

5 Pathways to Mystical Experience

1. Spontaneous Experiences

Mystical experiences may arrive without invitation or preparation. People report them while listening to music, walking in nature, grieving, giving birth, making love, or recovering from illness. The experience may last only moments and may remain memorable for decades.

2. Meditation and Spiritual Practice

For thousands of years, people have sought unity and transcendence through meditation, prayer, chanting, fasting, silence, and ritual. Buddhist monks, Christian contemplatives, Hindu yogis, and Sufi mystics have developed practices that encourage profound changes in awareness. Their traditions provide centuries of descriptions of similar experiences, interpreted in different ways.

3. Psychedelic Experiences

Psychoactive plants and fungi have long been used in spiritual ceremonies. Ayahuasca, psilocybin mushrooms, and mescaline-containing cacti can dramatically alter perception, emotion, and the sense of self.

Modern research has brought these experiences into medical settings. Griffiths et al. (2016) studied psilocybin-assisted treatment among people with life-threatening cancer, finding substantial reductions in depression and anxiety. Participants sometimes described experiences of extraordinary significance, including changes in their sense of identity and connection to the world.

4. Near-Death Experiences

People who have come close to dying sometimes describe radiant light, deceased relatives, profound peace, life reviews, and extraordinary love. Some report entering a reality more real than everyday existence. Modern resuscitation technologies have increased opportunities to collect accounts from survivors of life-threatening emergencies (Greyson, 2021; van Lommel, 2010; Parnia, 2024).

5. Virtual Reality

A new pathway is emerging through immersive virtual reality. Unlike traditional virtual reality, which represents people as solid, separate figures, researcher David Glowacki and colleagues created a shared virtual environment in which participants appear as diffuse, pulsing forms of light. As these forms interact, participants can experience a profound sense of unity and interconnectedness, as though the boundaries separating them from others have disappeared. Research using the Mystical Experience Questionnaire found that participants' scores were comparable to those reported after moderate-to-high doses of psychedelics (Glowacki et al., 2020, 2022). (Glowacki et al., 2020, 2022).

Mystical Experiences as Global Meaningful Coincidences

Consider the range of circumstances in which these experiences occur. Someone spends years meditating in a monastery. Another receives psilocybin during cancer treatment. Someone survives cardiac arrest. A group enters a specially designed virtual world. Across different people, cultures, centuries, and methods, the recurrent reports of mystical experiences through five pathways ask what these recurrent reports suggest about humanity's future. I wonder whether these experiences reveal possibilities within us that ordinary awareness seldom brings into view. When one meaningful coincidence occurs in an individual's life, the person may ask what it means for their present and future. When similar experiences recur across humanity, we can ask those questions on a much larger scale.

What Might This Mean for Humanity's Future?

Imagine increasing numbers of people directly experiencing the love and interconnectedness mystics have described for centuries. Such experiences could influence their relationships with one another, their communities, and the natural world. Our societies emphasize national, religious, political, economic, and personal differences. Yet mystical experiences offer glimpses of profound unity.

What if more people experienced that unity themselves? Could it influence how we educate children, resolve conflicts, organize communities, or care for the Earth? The possibility becomes especially intriguing as new pathways allow people who might never have sought a mystical experience to encounter one.

Meaningful coincidences are suggestions, not demands. They do not tell us what to do or guarantee a particular future. They invite curiosity about possibilities that might otherwise escape our attention. The global recurrence of mystical experiences may be one such invitation, suggesting that an extraordinary individual experience can also be part of a larger pattern unfolding across humanity.

The increasing reports of mystical experiences may be showing us what humanity could become.

item.title: Getting Straight to the Point About Postmodern Relativism
item.description:
Education

Getting Straight to the Point About Postmodern Relativism

Opinions are a natural part of consciousness, thought, beliefs, and discussions.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • From the first stone tools advancement has relied on consciousness, failures, and successes.
  • By questioning assumptions, and applying reason, this eventually helped establish the scientific method.
  • Excellence is not a product of wishful thinking. Excellence emerges through applied merit and competence.
Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

We have, since forever, had opinions. Opinions are a natural part of consciousness, thought, beliefs, discussions, and debate. This provides the means for everyone to express perspectives, challenge assumptions, agree to disagree, and explore possibilities. However, while opinions may stimulate inquiry, opinions alone do not create merit, enhance excellence, advance knowledge, or produce the achievements that have, as history informs, shaped civilizations (Dwyer, 2023; Ericsson, 2008).

History informs us that human progress has depended upon the discovery and application of objective sustained realities, i.e., universal truths, that exist independently of personal beliefs, opinions, or preferences.

Observations, Analysis, Testing, Failures and Successes

From the creation of the first stone tools to the application of the wheel, agriculture, the printing press, the scientific method, medicine, engineering, science, and, of course, much more, all manner of advancements have relied upon observation, analysis, testing, failures, successes, and the application of principles that consistently proved themselves to be reliable, which advanced skills, knowledge, understanding, insights, potential, and possibilities (Ericsson & Harwell, 2019; Krauss, 2024).

The philosophers, mathematicians, physicians, and scholars of ancient Greece and many other civilizations contributed through perseverance, resilience, constant study, and unrelenting personal application to the instructional, pedagogical, and educational principles of inquiry-based learning and associated achievements.

By continually critically questioning assumptions, applying reason, adhering to universal mathematical principles, and objectively investigating the natural world, all of these different civilizations helped to eventually establish the intellectual foundations that would later influence the Renaissance, the Age of Reason and Enlightenment, and ultimately lead to the development of the scientific method.

As such, it would be reasonable to declare that during these periods, increasing importance was eventually placed upon evidence, rational investigation, and the systematic critical examination of what could be later described as the existing empirical and quantifiable world (Ericsson, 2008; Krauss, 2024; Nouh, 2023; Yapijakis, 2009).

Skills, Knowledge, Insights, Understanding, and Learning

The social significance of this intellectual shift was profound. Skills, knowledge, insights, understanding, and learning itself became associated not merely with what people thought, perceived, or believed to be true, but with what could be observed, empirically examined, tested, and applied.

As noted, the scientific method emerged from this objective approach and provided a structured means through which thoughts, beliefs, and assumptions could be evaluated against observable reality. Ideas and opinions, as always, remained important, but ideas, perceptions, and opinions alone were not sufficient; they required research-based objective testing and verification.

The practical success of science, medicine, engineering, and technology has largely depended upon the systematic, quantifiable application of observation, testing, objective evidence, and critical inquiry. In this regard, claims about the existing world increasingly came to be evaluated not solely by belief, preferences, or opinions, but by their ability to withstand sustained empirical examination and objective verification (Atallah, 2018; Barz & Achimaș-Cadariu, 2016; Ghasemi et al., 2025).

The MACE Principle

This distinction becomes particularly important when considering the pursuit of excellence. Excellence is not a product of wishful thinking, preference, or opinion. Rather, excellence emerges through engagement with universal realities that govern learning, performance, and achievement.

One way of understanding this process is through what I refer to as the MACE principle. The pursuit of excellence requires Motivation, Application, Commitment, and Effort, and the actions of these four constructs contribute to Merit, Achievement, Competence, and Excellence.

Put simply, Motivation mobilizes Merit, Application advances Achievement, Commitment creates Competence, and Effort enhances Excellence. Research dealing with mastery, expertise, and deliberate practice consistently demonstrates that merit, achievement, competence, and excellence are developed through sustained engagement, repetition, perseverance, resilience, and continual refinement (Coyle, 2010; Datu, 2021; Ericsson, 2008; Ericsson & Harwell, 2019).

The broader lesson may be remarkably simple. We are all self-evidently free to have opinions, and opinions can, and do, serve a useful purpose in encouraging discussion and inquiry. However, opinions, beliefs, perspectives, and interpretations possess their greatest practical value when they are subjected to continuous analysis, examination, objective evidence, and unrelenting critical evaluation.

Source: Gerd Altmann/Pixabay

The Application and Adherence to Universal Principles

Throughout history, the advancement of skills, knowledge, understanding, competence, achievement, and excellence has depended not upon opinions, or what people preferred to believe, but upon the immutable application and adherence to universal principles that remain unchanged regardless of personal opinions or beliefs.

From the first stone tools to modern scientific achievements, skills, knowledge, and progress have been built upon this foundation. Gravity, arithmetic, geometry, physics, chemistry, thermodynamics, biological processes, and skill acquisition all function according to universal principles regardless of opinion.

As such, Postmodern Relativism opinions may begin a conversation, but, ultimately and immutably merit, achievement, competence, and excellence have developed and advanced through the self-motivated, disciplined pursuit of critical thinking and higher-order reasoning and the application of quantifiable universal truths, resilience, and perseverance (Atallah, 2018; Barz & Achimaș-Cadariu, 2016; Coyle, 2010; Datu, 2021; Ericsson, 2008; Ericsson & Harwell, 2019; Ghasemi et al., 2025).

item.title: Why You Need to Be the Hero in Your Own Life
item.description:
Personal Perspectives

Why You Need to Be the Hero in Your Own Life

Personal Perspective: Find the courage to take the lead and shape your destiny.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • People look to mythological archetypes to elevate their spirits and endure life with pride.
  • Transforming past disappointments and failures into bold acts of everyday courage is possible.
  • It's important to lean into opportunities to be generous and noble to assist in the betterment of others.

German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer wrote that “a happy life is impossible; the best that a man can attain is a heroic life.” I actually do believe that a happy life can be cultivated with patience and by maintaining a balanced perspective; however, let's look at this quote for a moment.

Why not consider being a hero in our own life journey? What if we interpret our everyday determination on an epic scale: for instance, how committed we are to our jobs, how protective we are of loved ones, and the risks we take to prosper and grow? Additionally, what if we lean into opportunities to be kind, generous, and noble that might assist in the betterment of others? What if we convert past failures or disappointments into daring acts of courage instead?

From his book Strength to Strength: Finding Meaning, Success, and Deep Purpose in the Second Half of Life, author Arthur C. Brooks writes that the legendary Greek warrior Achilles "had to decide whether to fight in the Trojan War, promising certain physical death but a glorious legacy, or return to his home to live a long and happy life, but die in obscurity." Achilles opts to fight and preserve his glory, which solidified his mythic immortality.

Although Achilles is a fictional character, like many mythological archetypes, they are meant to elevate our spirits, stir our souls, and help us bear the sufferings of life with pride instead of fear. They help us comprehend the natural world around us with wonder and curiosity.

Mythological characters are also intended to be extraordinary representations of our better selves. They are symbolic depictions of who we consciously or unconsciously desire to be. In essence, they help us tap into the warrior within us and inspire our hearts to be great at whatever we put our minds to. Sometimes, it means we have to make difficult decisions. Sometimes, it means we have to stand up and be courageous. Or maybe we have already, but we haven’t acknowledged it yet. Perchance, the greatness is just waiting to be recognized.

The key point here is, you don’t have to be a legendary Greek warrior to be a protagonist in your own life. You just need the nerve to author your own personal journey relative to your unique circumstances.

Writing Your Own Script: The Legacy of Lawrence of Arabia

In the 1962 film Lawrence of Arabia, British Lieutenant T.E. Lawrence, played by Peter O'Toole, is traveling by camel with a crew of Bedouin soldiers through the punishing Nefud desert. They are on a mission to capture the Turkish-occupied port city of Aqaba. They are traveling only by night, to avoid the merciless heat of the daytime sun.

One early morning, Lawrence sees a riderless camel drifting alone. He is immediately told that the man who has fallen behind in the darkness is his friend, Gasim. Lawrence, a bookish yet tormented social misfit dealing with depression and trauma, makes the sudden decision to ride back alone to rescue him. To his rageful guide, Sharif Ali, played by actor Omar Sharif, the choice is insane. Gasim does not stand a chance against the rising desert sun, and going back means death for both of them. To the audience, Lawrence's impulsive decision appears like a reckless act.

A livid Ali shouts at Lawrence, telling him “it is written” in the stars that Gasim’s fate is inevitable. He is a dead man already.

Many hours later, Lawrence returns triumphantly to the camp with Gasim clinging to his waist on the back of the camel. Ali, a convicted man of faith, is stunned by the miracle. As Ali hands him the waterskin to drink, Lawrence says to him. “Nothing is written.”

Question: Did Lawrence risk his life simply to prove Sherif Ali wrong? Was his decision a foolhardy gamble? Or a sincere heroic act? Irrespective of the inquiry, watching that scene always gives me goosebumps.

Since childhood, the film has inspired me to try to stay true to my convictions. It stirred me to take chances, assert myself more, and respectfully express my feelings without censure. Every time I watched the movie, I walked away feeling empowered to live my life better. I realized that perhaps I myself could write my own story of courage.

In conclusion, living in the heroic mode provides the highest aspiration to experience life selflessly, striving for good and perhaps even the benefit of others despite facing opposition. The heroic mode helps us endure pain with dignity and encourages acceptance of life and all its unpredictable twists and turns.

When I need to access motivation, I personally choose to channel my internal Achilles or T.E. Lawrence and go for the glory. I choose self-appointed nobility.

item.title: ADHD Has These Three, Sometimes Clashing Definitions
item.description:
ADHD

ADHD Has These Three, Sometimes Clashing Definitions

Different views of ADHD serve different purposes—and can all be valid.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • Three models define ADHD—clinical, biological, and social—but they are not competing truths.
  • ADHD traits may be advantageous in one environment and detrimental in another.
  • The most useful ADHD model depends on the person's needs at a particular moment.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is commonly defined by difficulties maintaining attention or with goal-directed behavior. While ADHD is commonly recognized as a disability, new ideas have started to emerge as to the origins and the nature of ADHD. While they all have some merit, they come from inherently different places.

The Clinical Model

The clinical view sees ADHD as a condition to be treated. Clinicians aim to identify what is wrong so they can treat it as efficiently as possible. The clinical view relies on the DSM diagnostic criteria to evaluate patients' treatment needs. One of the diagnostic criteria is that ADHD must significantly impair life to be diagnosed.

This means that the clinical model inherently sees ADHD as a deficit, or a condition, because the way it approaches it is with a treatment in mind. This can create issues, though, where individuals who appear "functional" are missed and don't receive the help they need because of compensatory mechanisms. This is where research clashes with diagnosis.

The Biological Model

In the biological model, ADHD is seen as a bundle of behaviors and traits that co-occur. It studies the biological origin, the traits that emerge, and where these traits may differ significantly from the population. The biological model, however, has no particular classification of good, bad, or impairing on these traits; it merely studies whether some things are different, and why.

Similarly, the biological model studies which conditions or environments can affect traits, and how. For example, a study showing that individuals with a similar DRD4 mutation experienced different outcomes as a function of the sedentarity or mobility of their environment. The biological model introduces nuance, saying that the same set of traits may be advantageous in one environment and detrimental in another.

This is why we also see the emergence of studies showing that people with ADHD perform better at a virtual foraging task than people without ADHD. Or that individuals with ADHD concentrate better with music than without music. Finally, we also see studies showing the correlation of ADHD with other conditions such as c-PTSD, which introduces an additional level of complexity.

The goal of all of these studies is eventually to make treatment and detection better, but initially it's merely about trying to understand how ADHD brains work, and what level of complexity exists in the heterogeneity of this particular neurotype.

The Social Model

Finally, ADHD is also an identity that co-exists within a dynamic and complex society. An ADHD diagnosis gives access to medication through clinical assessments. But the social dimension of ADHD also comes with changes in identity, self-perception, community, adjustments, rights, etc.

The social dimension of ADHD seeks to define it not as a disability, but as a difference. It considers the stigma and discrimination that go with it, and the need to reframe certain challenges so they can be more accepted by society at large.

The social model often distances itself from the clinical definition, and many people, in fact, end up refusing to call ADHD a disability or prefer to rename it as a "superpower" in the right conditions.

The Intersection

None of these views is inherently wrong. The clinical model is essential to help people find treatment. The biological model offers nuance and understanding—but is also the most complex to approach. The social model considers the complexity of human societies that require the participation of individuals with ADHD, and tries to make that participation as painless as possible.

Many conflicts, however, arise between people from these three worlds, who each believe their view is the correct one. The thing is, all three views are correct, but they serve different purposes. Understanding the purpose of each view is key to better understanding ADHD in its entirety. It is a complex neurotype that can have disabling consequences that require treatment. Its origins are multiple, difficult to track, and traits may change as a function of interventions, environments, or habits. Its place in society is still ill-defined, but a new language around it is also necessary to avoid stigma and discrimination.

In the end, it's not about who is right, but about which model is serving you at one specific moment.

item.title: The Biodiversity Crisis is Real and Must and Can be Fixed
item.description:
Environment

The Biodiversity Crisis is Real and Must and Can be Fixed

Kyle Harper uses the Sixth Extinction as a way to frame the conversation.

Posted October 20, 2026

Key points
  • "Shifting baseline syndrome" causes us to underestimate long-term biodiversity loss.
  • The Sixth Extinction is unique as humans are driving global species homogenization.
  • Human-driven extinctions compare to the most destructive events known from the fossil record.
  • It's not all doom-and-gloom, but it's going to take a lot of hard work to right the many wrongs.
Source: GN/Pexels.

It's surely not breaking news that we are ruining our lovely planet including air and water at an unprecedented rate. It can seem hopeless, but some people are offering a way out of what is called the Anthropocene—"the age of humanity"—that has morphed into what I call "the rage of inhumanity."

One such person is Dr. Kyle Harper who suggests a way to right the many wrongs in his highly-acclaimed new book The Last Animal: Human History and the Fate of Life on Earth from the Ice Age to the Sixth Extinction. In this important forward-looking book, Harper doesn't think the situation is necessarily a doom and gloom scenario; there is hope, but it going to take a lot of hard work. Putting the grand sweep of world history into geological perspective, Harper argues that the long view is essential to confronting the urgent challenges we face.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write The Last Animal?

Kyle Harper: Like anybody who spends years working on a project, I was motivated by a mix of personal and intellectual interests. The personal one comes from a concern about biodiversity. I grew up in Oklahoma and am now raising my kids here. But the animal world around them is notably different than the one I experienced as a child. The change is rapid and visible to the naked eye. To give one small example, I could (and did) catch Texas horned lizards with my grandfather at will. We saw them all the time. My kids have never seen one.

As a historian, I like to ask where things come from, and I wanted to deepen my understanding of how we got here. (And actually the story of these lizards is itself pretty incredible, once I started peeling back the layers of the onion). I think the biodiversity crisis is one of the most consequential and difficult challenges we face as a species, and I hope a deeper perspective can help us reckon with what we need to do to address it.

MB: How does your book relate to your background and general areas of interest?

KH: I am a historian by training, and my area of expertise is ancient Rome. But I love science and found a way to combine my interests, so I have spent a lot of time studying the history of climate change, human health and disease, etc. My overarching goal as a historian is to help us understand humanity’s place in the natural world. This project is inherently interdisciplinary, so I collaborate a lot with natural scientists in different fields.

Biodiversity is a subject that cries out for interdisciplinary work. Colleagues who come at the subject from the perspective of ecology or conservation biology are very interested in how history can contribute to our understanding, because they are well aware of the challenge of what is called “shifting baseline syndrome” - the difficulty of measuring human impact if we start counting e.g. extinctions or depletion in the relatively recent past. I came to feel that we really needed a book that moves across deep time, from our hunter-gatherer past to the high-tech present.

Source: Princeton University Press/with permission.

MB: Who do you hope to reach?

KH: I tried to aim the book at anyone curious about humanity’s place in nature. That might be anyone who is simply concerned about the biodiversity crisis to experts in fields that touch on conservation issues.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

KH: In the book I use the idea of the Sixth Extinction as a way to frame the conversation. The Sixth Extinction, as many already know, is the hypothesis that human-driven extinctions compare to the most destructive events known from the fossil record (most recently, the asteroid impact that killed off the non-avian dinosaurs).

I think the Sixth Extinction is a useful idea. Certainly, we have not yet caused anything like the number of extinctions that would qualify as a mass extinction event. Extinction rates are elevated relative to the historical baseline, which is hugely concerning, but it is tricky to measure and compare extinction rates. And yet, the value of the Sixth Extinction as an idea is to force us to take a very deep perspective.

I do think that the human impact will register as a major evolutionary turning point. In some ways, what is most telling is the contrast with the events in the fossil record. We are causing the first great homogenization in the history of animal evolution.

I also try to take a “systems” perspective. Species extinction is critically important, but it is important to remember that it is not the only kind of impact we care about. We can drive animals to ecological extinction without literal species extinction. Think of the bison: a herd of some 30 million animals roamed as the dominant herbivore on the Holocene grasslands, and these ecosystems are mostly gone. We need systems thinking to understand both past and present. I try to evoke some of the rich webs of life that existed in the recent past but that are now seriously damaged or endangered.

MB: How does your work differ from others that are concerned with some of the same general topics?

KW: First is its deep perspective. The biologist Barry Commoner called the first law of ecology the fact that “everything is connected to everything else.” The extinctions that transpired thousands of years ago are still reverberating. We misunderstand our impact, and the nature of the challenge, if we only think on timescales of a few decades.

Second is the effort to integrate human history into the story. By this I mean the history of social and technological development, marked by some familiar milestones - the control of fire, the invention of projectile hunting weapons, the domestication of plants and animals, the rise of cities and trade, the tapping of fossil energy, and the rise of synthetic chemistry. I try to look at these developments ecologically.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about how humans had a significant effect on the lives of countless other animals they will reconsider how we are living now and what can be done to foster more peaceful coexistence with them?

KW: Absolutely. As a historian my responsibility is to faithfully reconstruct the past. There is no denying that this can be unpleasant to encounter. I think that an honest assessment of how we got here is fundamental to understanding where we want to go. Our eyes naturally adjust to the dimming light, and I think we can too easily come to accept an impoverished natural world as normal. I hope to open our eyes by evoking the brightness of past ecosystems, which is how we start to see clearly.
